problem: Social robot navigation algorithms are usually evaluated in oversimplified scenarios (sparse, cooperative, obstacle-free crowds), so it is unclear how they perform under realistic complexity. Density is often used as the sole proxy for scenario complexity, and the other contributing factors are not understood.
motivation: Standardized benchmarks for social navigation need community understanding of what makes a scenario hard. The authors review the evaluation practices of ICRA/IROS/CoRL/RSS papers from 2015 to 2024 and find that most use low density, passing-only, large open rooms and cooperative agents. This leads to observations such as a blind constant-velocity robot doing well.
key_idea: Define complexity empirically as whatever factor causes a performance drop, then manipulate contextual factors (density, directionality, environment width, agent policy mixture) one at a time in simulation across a range of navigation algorithms.
insight: Density and narrow environment width correlate most strongly with performance drops, e.g. density vs success Spearman rho=-0.878. Heterogeneity is not inherently harder: mixed ORCA/SFM and passing+crossing scenarios were easier than ORCA-only or crossing-only. The learned and predictive methods (RGL, MPC/MPPI-SGAN) degrade sharply once density moves away from their training or tuning density (0.05-0.10), while simple reactive planners do well at low complexity, so evaluations at low complexity hide these failures.
method: Literature review: tabulates density, directionality, environment, robot size, max speed, kinematics, sensors and viewpoint for about 40 papers, separating contextual from robot-related factors.
Scenario formalization: a scenario is the tuple S=(n, A_R, A_1:n, s_R, g_R, s_1:n, g_1:n, pi_1:n, W_obs).

Base scenario and single-factor manipulation: 15 agents, 10x10 m room, ORCA/SFM agents at 1.0 m/s, passing and crossing. One factor is varied at a time: density 0.05-0.35 agents/m^2, width 4.5-1.5 m, directionality (5 types), policy mixture (SFM, ORCA, Mix1-3 with CV and static agents).
Algorithms evaluated: RGL (RL with a GNN), MPC-SGAN, MPC-CV, MPPI-SGAN, a reactive planner, ORCA, SFM and CV.

Metrics and statistics: success, time to goal, minimum distance to agents and path irregularity, averaged over 500 scenarios per condition with a fixed seed. Spearman correlation tests are used to test hypotheses H1 and H2.
Implementation: SGAN pretrained on UCY Zara, RGL retrained on 5 ORCA agents (the only setting that yielded a collision-avoiding policy), and an enhanced CrowdNav simulator.

setting.backbone: Mixed set of evaluated planners: RGL (RL + GNN, trained), MPC/MPPI with Social-GAN predictions (pretrained on UCY Zara), and classical ORCA, SFM, CV and a reactive planner
setting.training_data: Analysis study, no new model. RGL is retrained in CrowdNav simulation with 5 ORCA agents; SGAN is pretrained on the UCY Zara subset.
setting.observation: Perfect state information about agents in a 2D simulator (no sensor noise, circular agents)
setting.action_space: Continuous 2D velocity / CrowdNav discrete-holonomic action space (as in RGL)
setting.privileged: Perfect sensing of all agents' positions and velocities

numbers_note: Results are given only in figures (Fig. complexity_results) plus a few Spearman correlations in the text; there is no results table with SR/SPL for any standard benchmark.
results: Density correlates strongly with success rate (rho=-0.878) and minimum distance (rho=-0.760). Width correlates positively with success (rho=0.641), policy mixture negatively (rho=-0.778) and directionality moderately (rho=-0.524). This supports H2 fully and H1 partially. RGL beats the MPC/MPPI methods in nearly all experiments, especially at high density, and roughly mirrors ORCA success with larger minimum distances.
limitations: Simulation only, with perfect sensing, circular constant-size agents and cooperative agents modeled only by ORCA/SFM; no real-world validation or user-centered metrics.

Only contextual factors are studied. Robot factors (kinematics, sensors, viewpoint) are left to future work, and only algorithms with open-source implementations were tested, with tuning that could be better.
RGL failed to train in most settings (only the 5-ORCA setting worked), and the complexity notion is empirical rather than formal.
